title: Hierarchical Time-Aware Eviction with Prefix Cohorts for GPU KV Cache
creator: Ariana Costa
description:
Problem: As continuous batching increases request concurrency, the GPU KV cache experiences fragmentation and uneven prefix retention. Current global LRU/TTL heuristics either over-evict hot prefixes (hurting tail latency) or retain cold prefixes (wasting GPU memory). We need an eviction policy that (1) preserves correctness for prefix-scoped KV entries across concurrent batched requests, (2) minimizes 99th-percentile latency regressions, and (3) reduces worst-case memory footprint without requiring large static reservations.

This ticket scopes design and implementation of a hierarchical, prefix-cohort-based eviction policy that combines TTL decay, cohort-weighted LRU, and admission/leaky-bucket controls to align cache lifetime with workload patterns while providing correctness guarantees for prefix isolation and atomic invalidation.
proposal:
High-level algorithm:
- Partition KV entries into prefix cohorts using the request prefix hash (cohort = top-N bytes of prefix id). Cohorts are moderately sized to balance locality and agility (configurable; default 256 cohorts per shard).
- Each cohort maintains two soft watermarks (warm, cold) computed from recent hit-rate and observed sequence-length distribution.
- Eviction priority: (1) TTL-expired entries within cold cohorts -> remove first; (2) within warm cohorts, apply cohort-local LRU trimmed by per-cohort budget; (3) global fallback: weighted LRU where weight = inverse(hit_rate + alpha * cohort_activity).
- Admission control: leaky-bucket credits per cohort to limit immediate KV writes from hot spiky prefixes. Credits replenish based on observed throughput and available global memory. This prevents a single prefix from filling a shard during bursty batching.
- Correctness safeguards: versioned tombstones + optimistic sequence checks ensure that an entry removed concurrently with an in-flight batch is never re-used for a different prefix without explicit invalidation. Eviction records are written with a monotonic generation ID for the shard to allow clients/serving threads to detect stale caches.

Strong guarantees targeted:
- Prefix isolation: eviction cannot make a later request observe KV entries belonging to a different prefix generation (monotonic generation + tombstone applies).
- Forward progress: eviction ensures that admission and reclamation interplay does not deadlock (leaky-bucket fallback to global reclaim when memory pressure high).
- Batching safety: multi-request batch paths check per-request generation stamps before using cached KV to avoid cross-request contamination.
implementation_plan: Draft spec + microbench design: finalize cohort sizing, watermark heuristics, and credit algorithm (2d).
Prototype in dev branch: implement per-shard cohort metadata, TTL buckets, cohort-local LRU queues, and leaky-bucket admission counters (3w).
Unit tests: eviction ordering, tombstone/generation semantics, and race injection tests for concurrent batch admission (1w).
Integration tests: run end-to-end benchmarks with continuous batching harness + memory fragmentation simulator; validate 99p latency and memory goals (1w).
Canary rollout behind feature flag: enable on 10% of serving fleet, monitor eviction churn, tail latency, and OOMs (2w).
Production rollout and postmortem: expand to 50%/100% with rollback criteria and dashboards (1w).
acceptance_criteria: Unit tests cover: cohort membership, TTL-priority eviction, cohort-local LRU behavior, tombstone/generation checks, and admission credit exhaustion paths.

Integration bench: under representative continuous-batching trace (median batch size >= 8, bursty prefixes), memory footprint reduced by >= 18% vs baseline for same hit rate, and 99th-percentile latency regression <= 5%.
No reproducible cross-prefix KV contamination in chaos tests that inject concurrent evictions during multi-request batches.
Feature flag metrics: eviction churn, per-cohort hit-rate, admission-block rate, and generation tombstone errors are visible in Console; alert thresholds configured.
Canary stability: no increased OOMs or increased tail-SLO breaches during 72h at 10% fleet share.
notes: Cohort sizing trade-off: more cohorts => finer locality, higher metadata cost; fewer cohorts => coarse isolation but lower overhead. Default 256 chosen by early microbench to balance metadata bytes vs hit-rate gains.
We prefer soft watermarks so transient bursts can reclaim from TTL expiry rather than immediate cross-cohort evictions; this reduces tail latency from hot prefix oscillation.
Tombstone approach: lightweight generation ID per shard (64-bit) avoids storing per-entry version in hot path; we record generation on write and check-only in read path when eviction races occur.

This design intentionally avoids global locking: all cohort metadata updates are per-shard and use atomic ops where possible. Global weighted-LRU fallbacks are computed via periodic sampling instead of synchronous global state updates.
risks: Complexity: more moving parts increases maintenance burden; mitigation: strong test coverage and feature-flagged rollout.
Metadata overhead: cohort state increases GPU-host pinned memory; mitigation: compact counters (u32/u16) and optional cohort count tuning per deployment class.
Incorrect tuning could starve low-volume but latency-sensitive prefixes; mitigation: conservative defaults and ability to pin prefixes (pinlist) via Console for enterprise users.

Race windows around eviction + batch reads could cause false negatives in tombstone checks if not thoroughly tested; mitigation: targeted race-injection CI and a short-term conservative fallback to global reclamation under ambiguity.
Interaction with continuous batching: admission throttling may increase request queuing; mitigation: integrate with batch scheduler to surface backpressure instead of silent drops.
